name: VoiceAssistant-Eval
description: A comprehensive benchmark designed to assess AI assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing. It comprises 10,497 curated examples spanning 13 task categories, including natural sounds, music, spoken dialogue, multi-turn dialogue, role-play imitation, and multimodal image-audio tasks.
creator: Ke Wang; Houxing Ren; Zimu Lu; Mingjie Zhan; Hongsheng Li
citeAs: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li. VOICEASSISTANT-EVAL: BENCHMARKING AI ASSISTANTS ACROSS LISTENING, SPEAKING, AND VIEWING. arXiv:2509.22651v1, 2025.
rai:dataCollection: VoiceAssistant-Eval was constructed to evaluate voice assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing. The benchmark is organized into three main subsets: Listening, Speaking, and Viewing. For listening, the authors collected source data from 23 audio understanding datasets and converted collected text instructions into audio. For speaking, they pre-designed eight sub-tasks and used role profiles and question texts from RoleBench plus source data from 22 datasets, including 11 text datasets and 11 audio datasets. For viewing, they selected MMMU as the source dataset and paired images with audio tasks. The authors first extracted diverse visual and auditory inputs from 37 datasets, including natural sounds, music, dialogue, and various images. They synthesized spoken prompts using TTS models, evaluated and filtered synthesized clips, de-duplicated content, filtered incomplete or inappropriate items, categorized remaining examples into 13 task categories, and applied balanced sampling to equalize category representation.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, Experiments
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data come from 37 source datasets. Listening uses 23 audio understanding datasets spanning speech, sound, music, and general audio. Speaking uses RoleBench role profiles and question texts plus 22 datasets, including 11 text datasets and 11 audio datasets. Viewing uses MMMU as the image source dataset. The benchmark also includes synthesized speech instructions and 300 role audio clips reused as prompt audio.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors converted collected text instructions into audio; replaced image reference tokens with descriptive phrases; rewrote text with Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct to make it more suitable for TTS; rephrased multiple-choice options for readability; synthesized speech with three TTS models; evaluated generated speech with UTMOS Strong and regenerated clips until the score surpassed 3.8; transcribed synthesized audio with Whisper-Large-v3 and selected the sample with the lowest word error rate; de-duplicated questions using lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance with manual review; categorized items into 13 predefined task categories; and sampled data to balance task ratios.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing included replacing special image tokens such as "<image1>" with descriptive phrases, rewriting text for TTS suitability, rephrasing multiple-choice options for readability, synthesizing spoken questions, evaluating synthesized speech quality with UTMOS Strong, retranscribing synthesized audio with Whisper-Large-v3, selecting audio with the lowest word error rate, deduplicating candidate questions, excluding incomplete or unsuitable instances such as corrupted images, silent audio, ill-posed prompts, and demonstrably incorrect answers, and balancing the final sample distribution across 13 task categories.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Manual review was used during data curation. Suspected duplicates flagged by lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance were manually reviewed and removed. Curators reviewed candidate items in a web-based curation tool and assigned Good or Bad verdicts with optional notes. Manual review checked media integrity, task well-posedness, and answer validity. In addition, human judges independently evaluated 10% of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B responses from each of the 13 tasks for validation of the automated evaluation scheme.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For deduplication, suspected duplicates were flagged automatically and then manually reviewed. For evaluation validation, 10% of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B responses from each of the 13 tasks, totaling 1,050 examples, were independently evaluated by human judges. The paper reports Pearson correlation coefficients between automated and human evaluations ranging from 0.73 to 1.00 with an overall correlation of 0.92, and an overall agreement rate of 96.1%.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct; UTMOS Strong; Whisper-Large-v3; gpt-oss-20b; emotion2vec; Wespeaker
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors state that they will release both the dataset and evaluation code. They will maintain a data governance process for auditing and removal and reserve the right to update assets if consent or licensing concerns arise.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker voices and role audio clips are included for role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation. The paper also mentions five Chinese roles in the role-play task, while all other prompts and evaluations are in English.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to facilitate research on evaluating voice assistants and developing next-generation multimodal AI assistants. The paper emphasizes risks related to role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation, including identity spoofing, harassment, fraud, impersonation, privacy violations, and unequal performance across demographics. The authors propose safeguards including prohibiting training or releasing models intended to reproduce identifiable speakers without documented consent, requiring consent gating and watermarking or traceability of synthetic audio, providing safety cards, and maintaining governance for auditing and removal.
rai:dataBiases: The paper states that VoiceAssistant-Eval may carry biases from its source data and design choices. Questions and contexts are drawn from academic or synthetic sources, such as existing datasets and rewritten instructions, which might not reflect the full richness or fairness concerns of real deployments. The role-play subset uses a fixed set of 100 roles and associated style prompts, and these roles may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas. The benchmark is also largely monolingual, with all prompts and evaluations in English except five Chinese roles.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes several limitations: the 10.5K-item dataset may still be limited in diversity; all prompts and evaluations are in English except five Chinese roles, limiting generalization to diverse linguistic settings; only a limited range of models was evaluated, with just one proprietary system; the evaluation methodology relies on automated measures and GPT-based scoring that may introduce noise and bias; the benchmark may inherit biases from source data and design choices; the role-play subset may encode stereotypes or omit important personas; task coverage excludes video-audio integration and continuous audio-visual streaming; and the benchmark evaluates models offline and does not measure latency, partial utterance handling, barge-in, or error recovery.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating voice assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing, and for benchmarking model capabilities, safety, robustness, personalization, hands-free interaction, and multimodal understanding. The paper states it is intended for researchers to better evaluate voice assistants and facilitate future studies in this area. It is not supposed to be used for training models for cheating. The benchmark supports transparent, longitudinal assessment of system capabilities.
